messages.subject: Posterior predictive distribution
parts:
Hi,

Suppose there are two sets of data: training data {y_train, x_train} and testing data {y_test, x_test}. I am trying to understand how to obtain posterior predictive distribution for y_test given x_test and a model estimated using the training data.

I find the wells_predicted.stan example relevant. If I understand it correctly. its generated quantities section provides posterior distribution for y_train. To obtain the posterior distribution for y_test (the unseen data), I am wondering if I just need to declare testing data {y_test, x_test} in the data section and loop over the testing data in the generated quantities as the example code does.

Another question I have related to the following quote from the stan 2.4 manual (pp 340, Predictive Inference):

[start quote]
p(y_tilde | y) = integrate_Θ p(y_tilde|θ) p(θ|y) dθ
Here, both the original constants and predictors x and the new constants and predictors x_tilde are implicit.
[end quote]

Can anyone explain why the the new constants and predictors x_tilde has to be implicit? Is it just to simplify the notation here or we don't normally consider new constants and predictors in predictive inference?


Thanks for any suggestions,
Yu-Kai

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior predictive distribution
parts:
On Oct 15, 2014, at 6:40 PM, Yu-Kai Lin <ykl...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> Suppose there are two sets of data: training data {y_train, x_train} and testing data {y_test, x_test}. I am trying to understand how to obtain posterior predictive distribution for y_test given x_test and a model estimated using the training data.
>
> I find the wells_predicted.stan example relevant. If I understand it correctly. its generated quantities section provides posterior distribution for y_train. To obtain the posterior distribution for y_test (the unseen data), I am wondering if I just need to declare testing data {y_test, x_test} in the data section and loop over the testing data in the generated quantities as the example code does.
>

Yes.

There's a section in the manual titled "Prediction, Forecasting, and Backcasting"
in the regression chapter of the manual.

You can also do the predictions in the model block if they're too complicated
to do with simple random number generators. It's just more efficient to put
them in generated quantities.

> Another question I have related to the following quote from the stan 2.4 manual (pp 340, Predictive Inference):
>
> [start quote]
> p(y_tilde | y) = integrate_Θ p(y_tilde|θ) p(θ|y) dθ
> Here, both the original constants and predictors x and the new constants and predictors x_tilde are implicit.
> [end quote]
>
> Can anyone explain why the the new constants and predictors x_tilde has to be implicit? Is it just to simplify the notation here or we don't normally consider new constants and predictors in predictive inference?

Yes, just to simplify notation. The manual follows the notation in
the early parts of Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis book. I should
just go in and make the x explicit to avoid any confusion. We did that in
the very beginning of the Stan manual, which also used to drop the x.

- Bob
